studies.title: When The Sun Is Wound Up
studies.meaning: Five clauses open the surah and none of them finishes a sentence. Each begins with the same word for when, and each pairs a familiar noun with a passive verb of undoing. The sun wound up like cloth, the stars losing their light, the mountains moved off, the pregnant camels left untended, the wild animals herded together. The list holds the reader in suspense for thirteen ayat before any main clause arrives, which is the surah's method rather than an accident of style.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan and early. The commentators treat this opening as one of the passages that shocked the first audience most, and the tradition preserves reports of Meccans reacting to its recitation. No occasion is reported. What makes the list land is that four of the five items are things a person in that valley could see on an ordinary day, and one of them, the untended camels, could only mean a disaster in the household that owned them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for winding a turban round the head or coiling rope. It occurs once in the Quran, and the image is of light being gathered in and wrapped rather than of a fire going out.
Specifically she-camels ten months gone, the single most valuable animal a family could own. The word occurs once in the Quran and names the one possession nobody would ever leave unattended.

Beasts that live apart from people, defined by their avoidance of human company. Gathering them is a reversal of what the word itself means, so the line describes an animal behaviour that cannot happen.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A she-camel in her tenth month was the family's future: milk, a calf, and a store of value that could be traded for anything. She was watched constantly, kept near, and never left to wander. Anyone hearing that such animals had been abandoned understood immediately that whatever had happened was not a storm or a raid, because both of those were things you saved the camels from first.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the words in these five lines occur nowhere else in the Quran: the verb for winding the sun up, the noun for the pregnant camels, and the noun for the wild beasts. The surah's opening also holds twelve of these clauses in a row before any main clause arrives, and when it comes it is four words long.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says nothing directly about God, and no agent is named in any of the five lines. Every verb is passive, so the reader is shown effects and left to supply the cause, which is a different rhetorical situation from being told. What is established is the fragility of the fixed points people navigate by: light, landmarks, property and the boundary between wild and tame all fail in five lines.

crossReferences.why: Opens the following surah with the same construction and four parallel clauses of undoing.
Gives a similar list of stars put out and mountains blown away, in the same clipped form.
Shows the mountains moved and the earth left exposed, with everyone gathered and nobody left out.

studies.applyIt: Name the three things you unconsciously treat as fixed points during a normal day: the light you wake to, the route you take, the person who will be there in the evening. Just list them, on paper if you like. This passage works by removing exactly that kind of item, and it works better when you have named your own first.

studies.title: For What Crime Was She Killed
studies.meaning: The list continues and then breaks. Seas set boiling, souls paired off with their kind, and then a question is put to a murdered infant girl. The grammar is careful: she is the one asked, not her killers, and the question is about the crime she was supposed to have committed. It has no answer, and none is given. Then the sequence resumes as though nothing had happened, with the records spread open, but the reader has just been shown what will be on them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The burial of infant daughters is attested in pre-Islamic Arabia, though the sources indicate it was practised by some families rather than universally, driven by poverty and by shame at a daughter's birth. The Quran returns to it in several places, describing the father's face darkening at the news. Here it appears without argument or prohibition, simply as an item on the docket of the last day.

keyTerms.note: From a root about stoking an oven. Classical readings take it as the seas set alight, made to overflow, or emptied, and the sources record the range without deciding among them.
To join a thing to its like. Commentators read it as souls returned to bodies, or as people sorted into kinds and joined to their own sort, so the pairing is either reunion or classification.
A passive participle from a verb about weighing something down until it is crushed. The word occurs once in the Quran and describes the act by its physical method rather than by naming it a killing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A daughter in a hard year was a mouth to feed who would not fight, would not raise the household's standing, and whose marriage might one day tie the family to rivals. Some fathers responded to the news of a birth by withdrawing from company for days. The practice was not universal and it was known to be shameful, which is why it was done quietly and why poets of the period could use it as an insult.
studies.didYouKnow: The question in this passage is addressed to the victim rather than to the killer, which is grammatically unusual and was noticed early. The commentators explain that asking her is the sharper indictment, since she must answer that she had done nothing, and the man responsible is left standing there listening. No sentence is pronounced in the passage at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A crime that had no legal remedy in that society, committed against a person with no standing to complain, is placed on the record of the last day beside the collapse of the sun and the seas. The scale is the argument. And by questioning the victim rather than the perpetrator, the passage makes the record itself the instrument of justice: what is needed is not a prosecutor but a hearing.

crossReferences.why: Describes the father's face darkening at the news of a daughter and the choice he weighs afterwards.
Addresses the fear of poverty behind the practice and answers it with the promise of provision.
Lists the killing of children out of poverty among the things laid down for every community.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose suffering nobody in your circle counts as a real grievance, because they have no standing to press it. You may not be able to fix it. But you can be the person who says out loud, once, that it happened and that it was wrong. This ayah works entirely by giving a hearing to someone who never got one.

studies.title: What Each Soul Brought Along
studies.meaning: The last four clauses finish the list and the sentence finally lands. The sky is stripped off like a hide, the fire is stoked, the garden is brought close, and then, after twelve suspended clauses, four words: a soul knows what it has brought. Not what it did, and not what it will be told. What it produced and has with it. Then a new oath series begins immediately, and the surah changes direction without pausing on the verdict it has just delivered.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators note that the whole opening of the surah is one grammatical sentence, and that its main clause is far shorter than the conditions leading to it. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The audience were people accustomed to oral poetry with long suspended openings, so the technique was familiar even where the content was not, and the delay before the answer was itself part of the argument.

keyTerms.note: The verb for flaying a hide from a carcass or scraping a skin clean. It occurs once in the Quran, and it makes the sky a covering removed from something rather than a structure that collapses.
From a root about approach and closeness in rank. The garden does not receive people; it is moved toward them, which puts the last motion of the passage on the side of what is given.
A causative from the verb to be present, so the soul is described as having made something present rather than as having done it. The deed arrives at the scene alongside its owner.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Skins were worked constantly. A hide was pulled off a slaughtered animal in one piece if you were skilled, and everyone had watched it done. The word used here of the sky is that word. It carries the sudden change of an inside becoming an outside, which is exactly what the following lines describe: two destinations that had been hidden are now simply in view.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah's opening is a single sentence twelve clauses long, and its main clause is four words. The verb chosen there means to bring something present rather than to perform it, and the identical construction opens the answer in the surah that follows this one, where a soul knows what it sent forward and what it held back. Two adjacent chapters land on the same four-word form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The verdict is knowledge, not sentence. Nothing is announced to the soul; it simply knows, and what it knows is what it has with it. That makes the last day a disclosure rather than a trial, and it places the garden and the fire on the scene before the knowing rather than after it. Everything necessary is already present, and the only thing that changes is the seeing.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same opening verb and construction, a soul knowing what it advanced and what it left behind.
Describes the day each soul finds present before it whatever good and evil it has done.
Uses the same verb of the garden being brought near, and sets the fire in view alongside it.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what you would be carrying if today ended now, using the verb this ayah uses: not what you did, but what you brought with you. It is a slightly different question and it produces a slightly different list. Give it two minutes before sleep tonight, and do not extend it into a plan.

studies.title: The Night As It Turns
studies.meaning: Four oaths, and each names something at the moment it changes state. Bodies that withdraw and then sweep on and take cover, night at its turning, and morning as it draws breath. Scholars differ over the first pair, reading them as planets that appear to retreat, or as antelope that slip into their lairs, and the sources give both. What all four have in common is that they are named in transition, not at rest. Then the oath is answered, and the answer is about the origin of these words.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah is answering a specific charge current in Mecca, that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was speaking under some influence other than his own mind, and the commentators place the passage among the responses to that accusation. No occasion is reported for the oaths. The description that follows, of a messenger with rank and power near the Throne, is read by the great majority as a description of the angel who brought the revelation.

keyTerms.note: An intensive plural from a verb for entering a covert. Most commentators read it of stars that vanish at daybreak, others of antelope slipping into their lairs, and the sources keep both without choosing.

One of the Arabic words that carries two opposite meanings. The lexicons record it both for night coming on and for night departing, and the commentators divide accordingly, without either reading being ruled out.
The ordinary verb for drawing breath, used of dawn. It makes the first light an exhalation, and Arabic keeps the image alive: the same root gives the word for a soul and for something precious.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Travel across open country was navigation by sky. A guide knew which lights rose where, which of them wandered against the fixed pattern, and how far the night had gone by where they stood. Hunters read the other reading of these words: the hour when antelope go to ground. Both kinds of knowledge belonged to men who had spent whole nights outdoors and could tell the time by looking up.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used of the night in this passage is one of a small class of Arabic words that mean a thing and its opposite. The lexicons record it for night arriving and for night departing, and the classical commentators split on which is meant here, with neither side able to settle it from usage. The oath works either way, since both are moments of turning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The oaths are chosen for a reason that becomes clear only afterwards. Each swears by something caught between two states, and the claim they support is about a message in transit, carried from a throne to a human being by an intermediary described entirely in terms of position and trust. What is asserted is not the content of the revelation but the reliability of its transmission.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical clause about a noble messenger and then denies the alternatives being proposed.
Describes the same powerful and trusted bearer and the approach that followed, in more detail.
Names the trustworthy spirit as the one who brought the revelation down onto the heart, in clear Arabic.

studies.applyIt: Get up once this week for the few minutes when night is turning into morning, and watch it rather than checking a clock. The ayah swears by that exact interval. Most people have never seen it deliberately, only stumbled through it, and the difference between the two is the whole point of the oath.

studies.title: Your Companion Is Not Mad
studies.meaning: The bearer is described in four qualities and then the subject shifts to the man in front of them. He is called their companion, the word for someone they have lived beside, and the charge of madness is denied in a single clause. He saw the one who brought it, on a horizon described as clear. He is not stingy about what he was shown. And what he brings is not the speech of a driven-off spirit. Four denials, each answering an explanation the audience had already tried.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Every clause here answers a specific accusation recorded elsewhere in the Quran: that the message was the work of a possessed man, or a poet, or a diviner receiving whispers. The commentators note the choice of the word companion, which insists that the accusers had known this man for forty years before he said anything unusual. No occasion is reported for these particular ayat.

keyTerms.note: Not messenger or prophet but the ordinary word for someone you keep company with. It puts the accusation against a lifetime of shared streets and marriages, and the pronoun makes them the ones who know him.

The line where sky meets earth, the widest thing visible from one spot. Describing the sighting there places it at the limit of ordinary vision rather than in an interior state, which is the distinction the passage needs.

From a root about being sparing with something valuable. The classical readers preserve a second reading of this word, differing by one letter, which yields under suspicion instead of grudging, and both are transmitted.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was small enough that everyone's character was public property. A man's reputation for honesty was an economic asset, since caravan shares and deposits were held on trust with no courts to enforce them. Calling someone mad was therefore a specific commercial and social claim, not an insult, and it was the only available explanation for a person of known reliability saying something the city could not accept.
studies.didYouKnow: The word denying that he withholds the unseen is preserved in two canonical readings that differ by a single letter, giving either not grudging with it or not under suspicion regarding it. Both are transmitted from the earliest generations, and the commentaries record them side by side. It is one of the small number of places where a single dot changes the sense of a line.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The defence offered is not a miracle but a biography. The accusers are reminded that they know the man, that he saw what he reports at the edge of open sky, and that he has kept nothing back. Prophecy is thereby anchored in a public record rather than in a private claim, which is why the passage never argues about the content of the message at this point.

crossReferences.why: Denies that their companion has strayed or speaks from desire, using the same word for companion.
Invites them to reflect and see that their companion has no madness in him, in almost the same terms.
Answers the same three charges, that he is a diviner, possessed, or a poet awaiting misfortune.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone you know well whose account of something you have quietly discounted, not because of evidence but because the claim was inconvenient. The argument here is that long acquaintance is evidence. Go back to that person this week and ask them to tell you the thing again, properly, and listen to the whole of it.

studies.title: So Where Are You Going
studies.meaning: The denials end and the surah asks one short question with no object: where are you going. Then it drops every claim it might have made about itself and settles on the smallest one available. This is a reminder, for the worlds. The offer is opened to whoever among you wants to go straight, and then the last ayah closes the frame: and you do not will unless God wills. The two lines are left standing beside each other, and the classical tradition holds them together rather than choosing between them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah ends by turning from the accusations it has just answered to the audience's own position, which the commentators read as the point of the whole chapter: the opening catastrophes and the defence of the messenger both exist to make this question land. No occasion is reported. The closing pair of ayat became one of the most discussed passages in early theology, and mainstream commentary has consistently affirmed both.

keyTerms.note: The plainest word available for what the Quran is. It claims nothing about novelty: a reminder assumes the hearer already had the thing and mislaid it, which is a specific view of what revelation does.
From the verb to stand, in a form meaning to hold a straight course. It names the goal as direction rather than arrival, so what is offered is a way of walking rather than a destination reached.
The same verb is used of the human being and of God within a single line, deliberately. Nothing in the Arabic distinguishes them except the subject, which is what makes the ayah so much discussed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The question about where you are heading was a road question. Every journey out of Mecca began with a stated destination, because the route, the water stops and the season all followed from it, and a man who set out without one was a man in trouble. Asking a whole city where it thought it was going used the flattest possible language for something a caravan master settled before loading a single sack.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah closes on two consecutive ayat that appear to pull in opposite directions, one giving the choice to whoever wants it and the next placing all willing under God's will. The pair is repeated almost word for word at the end of another short Meccan surah, so the Quran states the difficulty twice rather than resolving it once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The Quran describes itself here at its most modest, a reminder rather than a proof or a law, and then leaves the human will and the divine will in one sentence without a joint. The classical tradition has read the two as complementary: the choice is real and it is not self-generated. Holding both is uncomfortable, and the text does not offer any relief from the discomfort.

crossReferences.why: Ends another surah with the identical pair, a way for whoever wills and then the will placed under God's.
Also calls the message a reminder for whoever wills, and then adds that they will not remember unless God wills.
Closes a long surah with the same claim, that this is only a reminder for the worlds, and its news will be known.

studies.applyIt: Answer the question in the surah literally, in one sentence, about the next five years. Where are you going. Most people find they can describe what they are doing but not where it leads. You do not have to fix the answer today. Writing down the honest version of it is the whole exercise.
